title: Language and translation registry
coverage_statement: This archive snapshot bundles canon-linked reader records for Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Jubilees, Enoch, Psalms plus 12 separately registered translation/companion layers. This is an availability count from reader records in this build, not a certification of completeness or textual accuracy; see each reader's review status. It records 22 language/script profile(s); these are scoped records, not an exhaustive world-language inventory. The coverage list contains 81 entries; 11 currently link to bundled source-text readers and 70 have no reader bundled in this archive. These are counts for this snapshot only, not a claim that no edition exists elsewhere. The registry also contains 59 unbundled translation, source-edition, or corpus leads. It also includes 42 separately scoped related research readers; they are not linked to or counted as Church-list book coverage. Unknown perspectives, text, boundaries, translation paths, and rights remain unresolved where the evidence does not establish them. Absence from this package means not bundled here; a zero is reported only for a defined, completed survey that found none; unassessed scope remains not surveyed or unknown, never zero by default. Machine-generated or unreviewed wording is not promoted to verified scripture, and missing texts or viewpoints are not synthesized.

translation_leads.edition: The Book of Jubilees, or The Little Genesis (A. and C. Black, 1902)
translation_leads.rights_status: Public-domain-marked scan; territorial exceptions require review
translation_leads.review_status: Bibliographic identity and OCR provenance are recorded; an OCR heading-pattern diagnostic found anomalies but does not verify chapter boundaries, completeness, or text accuracy. No line/page collation has been done. Territory-specific reuse remains uncleared.
translation_leads.notes: Google Books and Internet Archive describe the translation as made from Ethiopic; the IA item records the 1902 edition, 384 pages, and Tesseract OCR. A local OCR capture is preserved outside the public site with SHA-256 491e1726cdca207a4bc3a8b6877faed30cb43ba247246354567d43dfd84e35c5. Spot inspection finds commentary and page headers mixed into the body. It is not reader text and must not be represented as verified scripture. Commons marks the scan public domain in some jurisdictions but notes country exceptions; no global reuse conclusion is made. Local OCR diagnostic (same checksum and method): A diagnostic scan of the local 953,770-byte OCR capture (SHA-256 491e1726cdca207a4bc3a8b6877faed30cb43ba247246354567d43dfd84e35c5), using pattern (?im)^\s*CHAPTER\s+([IVXLCDM]+)\b, found 91 heading-pattern occurrences and 47 distinct Roman-token strings. It did not recognize IX, XXXIX, XLVI, or XLVII, and included the noncanonical token XXXL. OCR contents/page headers can create repeats or corrupt labels; these results do not establish missing chapters, chapter count, completeness, or boundaries. No OCR text is bundled.

translation_leads.review_status: WorldCat’s record for the 1912 edition states that Charles translated from the editor’s Ethiopic text and separately reprinted Greek fragments; the 1917 publication’s front matter says it reprints Charles’s 1912 translation. This supports the recorded immediate path gez → en at the edition-description level. The exact Ethiopic exemplar, full I–CVIII chapter sequence, completeness, wording, and alignment with the locally bundled Geʽez reader remain unaudited. Unbundled and not counted as reader coverage.
translation_leads.notes: The 1912 title specifies Ethiopic as the translation base and the Greek fragments as a separate reprint. “gez → en” describes that edition’s stated immediate basis; it does not prove Charles used the same Ethiopic recension as the archive’s local reader or that the two texts align. The 1917/1962 Gutenberg transcription visibly ends with a chapter heading CVIII, but the full chapter sequence, accuracy, and completeness have not been audited. Project Gutenberg marks the eBook public domain in the United States; local reuse law and any third-party edition restrictions must still be checked before bundling.
